scenes.tts: Put a pea plant in sterilised sand, and water it with a solution that holds no nitrogen. Add a little soil extract. The pea ends up with many times more nitrogen than its seed held. An oat plant in the next pot starves. Nitrogen gas makes up most of the air around both plants. So why can one use it and the other not?
scenes.visual: Two pots of sand under a nitrogen-free solution; the pea gauge climbs past its seed mark, the oat stays low, nitrogen gas fills the air above both.
scenes.narration: Put a pea plant in sterilised sand, and water it with a solution that holds no nitrogen. Add a little soil extract. The pea ends up with many times more nitrogen than its seed held. An oat plant in the next pot starves. Nitrogen gas makes up most of the air around both plants. So why can one use it and the other not?

scenes.tts: Hermann Hellriegel and Hermann Wilfarth tested this in pots, at an experiment station in Bernburg. They published in 1888. The solution held the other mineral nutrients but no nitrogen. The oats grew only as far as the nitrate they were given allowed.
scenes.visual: One oat pot; nitrate chips are added one by one and the oat plant and its gauge rise only as far as the nitrate.
scenes.narration: Hermann Hellriegel and Hermann Wilfarth tested this in pots, at an experiment station in Bernburg. They published in 1888. The solution held the other mineral nutrients but no nitrogen. The oats grew only as far as the nitrate they were given allowed.

scenes.tts: Now the peas. With no extract, they formed no nodules, and gained no nitrogen. Given a little extract of field soil, they formed nodules, which are swellings on the roots. These peas gained much nitrogen from the air. Extract that had been heated first gave no nodules and no gain. A living agent from soil, tied to the nodules, was required.
scenes.visual: Three pea pots side by side: no extract, live extract, heated extract; only the middle one grows nodules and its gauge rises.
scenes.narration: Now the peas. With no extract, they formed no nodules, and gained no nitrogen. Given a little extract of field soil, they formed nodules, which are swellings on the roots. These peas gained much nitrogen from the air. Extract that had been heated first gave no nodules and no gain. A living agent from soil, tied to the nodules, was required.

scenes.tts: The experiment did not name that agent. In the same year, Martinus Beijerinck reported isolating bacteria from nodules. They are called rhizobia. They enter the root. Inside nodule cells they become bacteroids. A bacteroid holds an enzyme called nitrogenase. Nitrogenase reduces nitrogen gas to ammonia. The root itself makes no nitrogenase.
scenes.visual: A nodule cell as a block: a rhizobium chip enters, becomes a bacteroid with a nitrogenase chip, nitrogen gas goes in and ammonia comes out; the root cell is marked as having none.
scenes.narration: The experiment did not name that agent. In the same year, Martinus Beijerinck reported isolating bacteria from nodules. They are called rhizobia. They enter the root. Inside nodule cells they become bacteroids. A bacteroid holds an enzyme called nitrogenase. Nitrogenase reduces nitrogen gas to ammonia. The root itself makes no nitrogenase.

scenes.tts: In return, the plant supplies carbon. Sucrose from the leaves is converted to malate, and malate fuels the bacteroids. Oxygen damages nitrogenase, yet the bacteroids respire. A plant protein called leghemoglobin binds oxygen and holds it at a low, steady level. It does not keep oxygen out. In Lotus japonicus, silencing it raised free oxygen in nodules, and fixation stopped. The plants grew normally only when given mineral nitrogen.
scenes.visual: Sucrose arrives, becomes malate and feeds the bacteroid; oxygen chips are bound by leghemoglobin to a low level; then leghemoglobin is silenced, oxygen floods in and nitrogenase is struck out.
scenes.narration: In return, the plant supplies carbon. Sucrose from the leaves is converted to malate, and malate fuels the bacteroids. Oxygen damages nitrogenase, yet the bacteroids respire. A plant protein called leghemoglobin binds oxygen and holds it at a low, steady level. It does not keep oxygen out. In Lotus japonicus, silencing it raised free oxygen in nodules, and fixation stopped. The plants grew normally only when given mineral nitrogen.

scenes.tts: Oats and barley have no nodules. They depend mainly on nitrate and ammonium in the soil. In those pots, oats had only the nitrate their solution held. A plant cannot make an element. It must take each one in, alone or with a partner.
scenes.visual: Oat pot with nitrate and ammonium only; pea pot with a bacterial partner and nitrogen gas; the rule appears below.
